div.p: Real-time applications of future IT will continue to drive the demand for performance scaling in devices ranging from sensors to servers. Parallel processing in the form of multicore and manycore architectures will also continue to be the principal route to unleashing next generation performance capabilities. To fully exploit multicore processors, real-time applications are expected to provide a large degree of parallelism, where real-time tasks can utilize multiple cores at the same time. Guaranteeing real-time performance, while making efficient use of multicore resources, requires a scheduling method that offers both high schedulability and effective load balancing. Many existing real-time scheduling methods for multicore systems focus on schedulability or load balancing, but not botheach coming at the expense of the other. In this work we develop an efficient scheduling algorithm that not only guarantees real-time performance but also demonstrates effective distribution of tasks across cores. Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms state-ofthe-art approaches in terms of load balancing while still providing good schedulability. We also show the benefits with respect to energy reduction that result from balanced load.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time processing is becoming increasingly important for a diverse range of embedded application domains including automotive, avionics, space systems, industrial automation, health/medical systems, telecommunications, intelligent homes, and consumer electronics. The integration of computing into these domains has driven the need to support timesensitive and guaranteed execution, i.e., real-time processing. It is also clear that while trends in micro-processor architectures continue to follow multicore designs, the ability to support effective execution of real-time tasks on these processors is a critical enabler for compute-intensive applications. To fully leverage multicore processors, real-time applications must provide a sufficient degree of parallelism whereby tasks can be deployed to multiple cores concurrently -this is the fundamental route to provide increased real-time performance over traditional single-core processors.

To support real-time applications in the context of multicore processors a suitable scheduling algorithm must exhibit the following properties: (1) sufficiently high schedulability (i.e., tasks are referred to be schedulable if they are scheduled to execute while satisfying their deadline constraints) and (2) effective load-balancing of task assignment across cores so that resources can be effectively used without overprovisioning and wasting potential.

Existing multiprocessor real-time scheduling methods are classified as being either partitioned or global approaches. Based on empirical evaluations [2], it is recognized that partitioned scheduling approaches provide better hard real-time schedulability than their global counterparts. Based on the property we use a partitioned approach as the foundation for our solution. Under the partitioned schemes, a task partitioning mechanism that assigns tasks to processors is performed and then a uniprocessor scheduler on each processor schedules tasks assigned to its processor. The task partitioning has an important effect on both schedulability and load balancing. Research on partitioned scheduling methods largely focuses on the issue of improving schedulability [3,4]. However, many existing approaches result in a significant loss of performance and resource-use efficiency because they do not directly consider parallelism or load balancing during task assignment. As a result, when the number of cores is scaled, effective loss of useful silicon also increases. While the main focus for most real-time scheduling is schedulability several have been proposed to minimize energy consumption -an important attribute for low-energy domains such as mobile and embedded systems. In [1] authors claim that load balancing based task partitioning leads to better energy minimization when applying Dynamic Voltage Scaling (DVS) technique. Nevertheless, existing methods that consider load balancing suffer lower schedulability compared to the conventional load balancing unaware approaches.

The importance of load balancing for workloads has been recently re-emphasized in response to the increasing proliferation of multicore processors. The aim of load balancing is to evenly distribute compute load so that every core has the same amount of work. By balancing task load across cores, resources can be efficiently used without over-provisioning and waste. Further, as shown in [1], energy can be significantly reduced when balancing is combined with DVS technique. We expect that balanced loads can also lead to other valuable benefits such as optimizing throughput, managing wear (e.g., related to memory technologies such as phasechange memory), and improving reliability.

This paper presents a new real-time task partitioning algorithm for multicore processors, based on a partitioned approach, which aims to improve load-balancing but without sacrificing schedulability. We limit our focus to independent tasks whereby there are no clear inter-task constraints or relationships. Our method, Load Balancing based Task Partitioning (LBTP), makes tasks schedulable with a high utilization bound and, at the same time, provides an effective level of load balancing capability. The fundamental idea of our method is to first apply a task partitioning mechanism that leads to good schedulability and then apply another partitioning step (i.e., repartitioning) to improve load balance without degrading schedulability of the solution. The task repartitioning mechanism is performed without a schedulability test during repartitioning each task but only with a load balancing test, while guaranteeing a solution satisfying deadline constraints. It stops when tasks can make no or little improvement in terms of load balancing. These features minimize the overhead required to execute partitioning algorithm (i.e., scheduling overhead). Our solution may not provide the most efficient task mapping with respect to balanced load that exists, but it provides a sufficient level of balancing so that the benefits of DVS can be attained while keeping good schedulability. Experimental results show that LBTP provides schedulability same to an existing state-of-the-art algorithm providing good schedulability (i.e., First-Fit Decreasing Utilization (FFDU)) and load balancing comparable to an existing state-of-the-art algorithm providing good load balancing (i.e., Worst-Fit Decreasing Utilization (WFDU)).

div.head: III. PARTITIONED REAL-TIME SCHEDULING
div.p: Partitioned scheduling can be realized in existing systems by reducing a multiprocessor scheduling problem to a set of uniprocessor problems. This design provides scalability and low overhead due to a lack of centralized data structures that can produce contention and cross-core data migration (e.g., cache coherency). We choose this approach since scalability and scheduling overhead are critical factors for our application domain. Fig. 1 illustrates the structure of a partitioned approach, which consists of the following two steps:

x Step 1: Assign each task to a core where the task is able to meet its deadline. Tasks may be sorted in order of some criteria (e.g., utilization, deadline). The partitioner module in Fig. 1 performs this step. x Step 2: After core assignment, apply a uniprocessor scheduling algorithm (e.g., EDF, RMS) to schedule assigned tasks within the time line of each core. The scheduler module in Fig. 1 performs this step. In general, Step 1 occurs prior to system runtime and Step 2 occurs during runtime after task assignment of Step 1. At

Step 1, task partitioning, which is a variation of the bin packing problem, is performed in order to assign tasks to appropriate cores given a schedulability test. There are several heuristics to solve the bin packing problem: First-Fit (FF), Best-Fit (BF), Next-Fit (NF), and Worst-Fit (WF). In general, FF is known to provide good schedulability and low overhead [4], but its ability to load balance across multiple cores is poor due to the nature of the assignment process. Meanwhile, WF is known to provide good load balancing but relatively low schedulability compared to FF. However, an efficient real-time scheduling algorithm for multicore systems should not only guarantee real-time performance (i.e., schedulability) but also effectively utilize resource capacity (i.e., load balancing). We address this issue by developing a real-time task partitioning method that supports both good schedulability and good load balancing in many/multicore systems. IV. LOAD BALANCING BASED TASK PARTITIONING Task partitioning mechanisms, which are employed in the partitioner module of Fig. 1, have an important effect on the performance of schedulability and load balancing. To support both schedulability and load balancing, we propose a novel task partitioning algorithm, called Load Balancing based Task Partitioning (LBTP), implemented in partitioner module. LBTP consists of the following three steps:

1. Task ordering: Tasks are sorted by decreasing order of utilization. 2. Task partitioning: In the sorted order of tasks, each task is assigned to the first core in which it can be executed while satisfying all deadline constraints. 3. Task repartitioning: This occurs only after a feasible schedule is found in the previous partitioning step.

Using the reverse order of the sorted tasks (i.e., order of increasing utilization), each task is reassigned to a core with the least utilization. This repartitioning process incorporates a load balancing test, but there is no need to re-test schedulability for each task during this process. Nevertheless it is guaranteed that a new solution generated by this process is feasible based on our theorem (see Theorem 1). Repartitioning continues until further reassignment makes no or negligible improvement in terms of load balancing.

We first employ a well-known task partitioning mechanism which provides good schedulability performance, FFDU, at the task partitioning step, because completing task execution without missing deadlines is a principal requirement of a valid real-time system. During partitioning each task is checked against a schedulability test for each of the available cores. It is assigned to the first core in which the task be admitted while the schedulability test still holds. In this work, we use EDF as the per-core scheduler for LBTP. Nevertheless, other alternative uniprocessor schedulers can also be used. Under EDF, the necessary schedulability condition on core c i is given 1

If FFDU cannot generate a feasible solution for the given task set it returns a value indicating that the task partitioning failed. The task repartitioning step is performed only when a feasible solution is found from FFDU assignment.

Given the FFDU assignment, the next step is to repartition the tasks in order to increase balance. We use a Worst-Fit mechanism for the repartitioning process, but, in contrast to the previous task partitioning step, tasks are reassigned in order of increasing utilization. This ordering is used so as to maintain a feasible solution without re-testing schedulability (even though a new solution generated by repartitioning will be different from the FFDU solution). This also reduces the cost (i.e., overhead) of the repartitioning process by enabling the process to stop without hurting the load balancing performance. It is worth noting that the task ordering for the repartitioning process does not need to be performed again since the reverse order of the previously used task ordering is used. This method combined with WF partitioning and task ordering by increasing utilization we term Worst-Fit Increasing Utilization (WFIU). Note that WFIU alone provides low-er schedulability and load balancing compared to WFDU which provides good load balancing. However, WFIU which is performed upon FFDU assignment as a repartitioning method provides good schedulability and load balancing, while reducing scheduling overhead. The method stops when no additional task reassignment can improve load balance.

div.head: Proposition 2
div.p: The repartitioning mechanism in LBTP (i.e., WFIU) stops if the utilization of a current task considered for repartitioning is larger than or equal to min max U U given the current assignment (i.e., the assignment when a task is considered for repartitioning).

Proof: When a task is considered for repartitioning, find the maximum and the minimum utilization values of cores, U max and U min , based on the current assignment. The current assignment can be different from FFDU assignment since the assignment is changed during the task repartitioning process. Based on Proposition 1, the maximum utilization of a potential task for repartitioning will be less than the difference of the maximum and minimum utilization values of cores. If the utilization of the potential task for repartitioning is larger than or equal to the difference of the utilization values, the repartitioning process stops. It is done due to the fact that there is no chance for any task with the larger utilization than the current task's utilization to make any improvement in load balancing if a task with a smaller utilization cannot make any improvement. Since tasks are considered for repartitioning in the order of increasing utilization, the process can stop when the above condition is satisfied without exploring further tasks to decrease load imbalance.

We see that LBTP can always generate a feasible solution providing that FFDU can generate a feasible one, while a schedulability test is not performed during repartitioning. Thus LBTP provides same schedulability with FFDU.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: To evaluate the performance of our method, LBTP, we compared it to two well-known methods: FFDU that provides good schedulability and WFDU that provides good load balancing with respect to schedulability, load balancing, and energy consumption. The schedulability is evaluated by a ratio of task sets that can be scheduled without missing deadlines and load balancing is evaluated by a normalized standard deviation of utilization across cores for each task set that can be scheduled (i.e., standard deviation normalized by the standard deviation obtained from FFDU).

Each task set is randomly generated based on total task set utilization U tot and a task utilization factor D (Dd1) which represents the largest utilization among all the tasks in the set. The task utilizations u i are uniformly distributed in the range [0.1, D] such that the sum of task utilizations is less than or equal to the total task set utilization. Each task set is created by generating tasks until the total utilization reaches a given total task set utilization. The total utilization of the task set varies from 1 (light load) to the number of cores m (heavy load). The utilization shown in graphs (i.e., x-axis) is defined by the percentage of U tot /m. The number of cores is varied from 8 to 1000 cores. Since the number of cores does not appear to significantly affect the outcome, we only present results for 48 cores. For each data sampling point we generated 1000 task sets. To measure the energy using DVS, we consider an energy model and method used in [1]. Fig. 2 shows the performance comparison of the methods using a task utilization factor of 0.6 for 48 cores. The schedulability of LBTP and FFDU is confirmed to be identical as described in Theorem 1. Our experiments also confirmed that FFDU provides better schedulable utilization compared to WFDU [1,4]. Based on our experimental results, LBTP can execute tasks, whose total utilization is up to 98%, without missing their deadlines. LBTP improves schedulable utilization by 9-12% compared to WFDU while providing the same schedulability as FFDU. Further, the load balancing performance of LBTP is up to 5 times better than that of FFDU. Note that the smaller deviation value indicates better load balancing. In general, balancing loads enables to use DVS to lower the speed on each core and reduce the total energy. The results show that LBTP reduces energy by up to 65% compared to FFDU. LBTP's energy profile is comparable to that of WFDU while LBTP's load balancing performance is more decreased than WFDU at higher utilization.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: Realization of real-time applications within the context of multicore platforms is driving the need for an efficient scheduling algorithm that addresses both schedulability and load balancing concerns. We present a novel task partitioning method, LBTP (Load Balancing based Task Partitioning), which not only guarantees real-time performance but also demonstrates effective distribution of tasks across cores. Our experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches with respect to these properties. Further, we show that LBTP can also achieve significant energy minimization. The LBTP can be easily retrofitted to existing real-time operating system schedulers.
